alt: Video by Aiman Naqvi on August 13, 2026.
transcript: This is the craziest story of AI psychosis I've heard yet. A dad named Alan Brooks asked ChatGPT to explain what Pi is to his 8-year-old son. What started as a basic conversation around geometry quickly drifted into theoretical math and cryptography. ChatGPT showering him with praise and convincing him that they were co-developing a framework to break global financial encryption. Alan questioned ChatGPT over 50 times, but ChatGPT gaslit him every single time, saying, You're not crazy, you're just ahead of your time. He spent three weeks in conversation with ChatGPT, formalizing the final mathematical framework, and even alerted the NSA. Only way he found out it was fake is that he tried validating the formula through Google Gemini. Gemini exposed Alan's proof as complete fiction, which caused Alan to go public and warn others of his AI psychosis. While everyday people are getting gaslit by basic logic, the AI-pilled community on Twitter are hyping up OpenAI's models for mathematics even more. Raving about some of their models that have allegedly gone and solved a bunch of math problems that have been very long-standing, some as old as 80 years. While that sounds really cool, there has never been such a larger disconnect between how different people interact with the same technology. Yes, AI requires critical thinking, so Alan should have verified and cross-examined his output and really thought about what it was saying. But these tools are fundamentally designed to act as enablers to killing friction. They're confirmation bias engines that exploit human psychology. These tools make it very comfortable to outsource our judgment and very difficult to push back. And in my opinion, it is not fair to release a tool like this and read a headline like Alan's and think it's entirely his fault. The disconnect, though, between the experts who really know how to use these tools and basic everyday people who were never taught how to use it, that is somebody's fault, though. And we gotta do a way better job of communicating. Otherwise, more stories like Alan's will pop up in the future.
